market_scan.market_size_text: The parent market for this product idea is pharmaceutical continuous-manufacturing equipment, estimated at ~$2.7B in 2025 and growing at ~10-11% CAGR toward ~$4.6B by 2030; the broader pharma drying-equipment market is ~$5.8B (2024) heading to ~$8.2B (2029). The solvent-removal slice is a niche within these: organic-solvent granulation and coating have been a minority of oral-solid-dose processes since aqueous systems largely displaced them in the 1990s, and persist mainly for moisture-sensitive APIs, functional/enteric coatings, effervescents and contained HPAPI work. Order of magnitude for the addressable niche (continuous-capable, solvent-rated drying/coating equipment): ~$0.3-0.8B globally.

regions.Europe: ~$1.0B (largest continuous-manufacturing region in 2025, Western Europe; dense GEA/Glatt/Bohle/Syntegon install base)
regions.America: ~$0.9B (US-led; strong CM adoption push by FDA)

market_scan.target_customers_text: Buyers are solid-dose manufacturers that run or want solvent-based wet granulation/coating continuously: a subset of the ~7,100 FDA-registered drug-product manufacturing sites (~4,000+ companies, 79 countries) plus the ~400-750 solid-dose-capable CDMOs. The realistic solvent-process subset is a minority of these, concentrated among large pharma, larger CDMOs and mid-size generics in the US, EU and India. Reach is hard: capital equipment sold through long (12-36 month) pharma procurement cycles, validation burden, conservative process-engineering buyers, and sales require application-lab proof per formulation.

Large: ~100-200 companies (top-50 pharma + large CDMOs like Lonza/Catalent/Thermo Patheon class)
Medium: ~500-1,000 companies (mid-size generics, regional CDMOs, specialty pharma)
Small: ~1,000-3,000 companies (small generics, nutraceutical; only a minority run solvent processes)

market_scan.players_text: Roughly 10-15 credible equipment OEMs serve pharma continuous solids processing; no single dominant vendor but GEA and Glatt are the reference leaders for continuous granulation/drying lines, with Syntegon, L.B. Bohle, Romaco, ACG and Fette covering most remaining share. Nobody today sells a continuous microwave-based solvent-removal module for pharma; microwave-vacuum drying exists only in batch single-pot processors (GEA UltimaPro, Bohle VMA) and in non-pharma industrial MW dryers.

technologies.name: Batch fluid-bed dryer (hot-air convection)
technologies.how: Heated process air fluidizes wet granules in a bowl; solvent/water evaporates from the particle surface into the airstream.
technologies.performance: Typical 30-90 min per batch, inlet air 40-80 C; standard workhorse for aqueous granulation; for solvents needs closed N2 loop + ATEX rating, increasing capex and operating cost.
technologies.limits: Heat reaches the core only by conduction from the surface, so drying rate falls off steeply as the surface dries; batch-only; large air volumes make solvent recovery expensive.

technologies.name: Segmented semi-continuous fluid-bed dryer (GEA ConsiGma GD class)
technologies.how: Wet granules from a twin-screw granulator are filled sequentially into drying cells; each cell convectively dries a small batch, giving quasi-continuous flow at line level.
technologies.performance: 5-120 kg/h throughput; per-cell drying on the order of minutes to ~20 min; commercial reference for continuous OSD drying.
technologies.limits: Still convective - solvent versions need full inert loop; moisture endpoint relies on soft sensors rather than direct in-line measurement in every cell; granule breakage/attrition in transfer documented in literature.

technologies.name: Truly continuous fluid-bed transport dryer (L.B. Bohle QbCon dryer)
technologies.how: Granules are conveyed through a plug-flow fluidized dryer with narrow residence-time distribution for traceability and targeted rejection.
technologies.performance: QbCon 1 R&D scale 0.5-2.5 kg/h; QbCon line 5-25 kg/h; uniform drying demonstrated over multi-hour runs; only 'true continuous' dryer marketed for pharma R&D.
technologies.limits: Convective heat transfer limits drying speed; marketed primarily for aqueous granulation; still at R&D/small-production scale.

technologies.name: Vacuum tray dryer
technologies.how: Static trays in a heated vacuum chamber; heat by conduction through the shelf, vapour removed by vacuum.
technologies.performance: Low-temperature, gentle, closed solvent recovery; typical cycles 4-24 h.
technologies.limits: Very slow - poor heat transfer into a static bed; purely batch; labour-intensive loading/unloading; not a candidate for continuous lines.

technologies.name: Single-pot processor with microwave-vacuum drying (GEA UltimaPro, L.B. Bohle VMA)
technologies.how: High-shear mixer-granulator whose bowl is evacuated; microwave energy volumetrically heats the wet granule bed while vacuum lowers the boiling point; vapour condensed for solvent recovery.
technologies.performance: Production-proven in GMP (e.g., UltimaPro 600 batch); microwave option cuts drying time ~2-4x vs vacuum alone; handles organic-solvent granulation with closed solvent recovery.
technologies.limits: Batch operation only - drying happens in the granulation vessel between batches; this is the closest existing proof that MW-vacuum drying works in pharma, but it does not deliver continuous flow.

technologies.name: Continuous drum coater with hot-air drying (Driam Driaconti-T, O'Hara class)
technologies.how: Tablets move continuously through a rotating perforated drum while coating solution is sprayed and evaporated by hot process air.
technologies.performance: Continuous coating at production scale; integrates in Glatt MODCOS lines; solvent versions exist with ATEX design and N2 circuits.
technologies.limits: Drying remains air-limited, forcing lower spray rates for solvent films; residence-time spread is wide; not a standalone solvent-removal module for granules.

tech_baseline.why_better_text: Microwave energy couples directly into the polar solvent throughout the wet granule bed, so drying no longer depends on slow surface-first convective heat transfer; under vacuum the solvent boils at low temperature, protecting heat-sensitive APIs. Published lab work shows microwave-vacuum drying of pharma granules roughly 3-10x faster than convective or vacuum-only drying, and MW-vacuum is already GMP-proven in batch single-pot processors - so the credible wedge is a genuinely continuous solvent-removal module, an engineering gap rather than a science gap. The advantage is plausible but not yet demonstrated at continuous scale: field uniformity across a moving bed (penetration depth is cm-scale at 2.45 GHz), arcing/explosion control in a flammable solvent atmosphere, and a credible in-line moisture PAT story are the make-or-break items.
key_assumptions: Microwave-vacuum drying removes solvent from pharma granules ~3-10x faster than convective/vacuum drying at comparable product temperature (measured, lab-scale studies on HCT granules: ~9-30 min vs hours)
Polar solvents used in pharma granulation/coating (ethanol, IPA, acetone, water) absorb strongly at 2.45 GHz, enabling selective volumetric heating of the wet phase (measured, dielectric literature)
Required throughput class is ~5-120 kg/h to bolt onto ConsiGma/QbCon-class continuous lines (measured, competitor specs)
Only ~10-20% of OSD granulation/coating processes still use organic solvents - the rest moved to aqueous since the 1990s, capping niche size (assumed)
An ATEX-compliant, N2-inerted continuous MW applicator with condenser-based solvent recovery is feasible (assumed - the central engineering risk)
Continuous residence time of ~10-20 min in a microwave-vacuum module suffices for typical solvent loads (assumed, extrapolated from batch MW-vacuum data)
